setting: A fictional panel interview for a {{role}} role at {{company}}, a mid-sized company.

presentation.situation: You are interviewing for a {{role}} role at {{company}}. {{lead}}, the hiring manager, and {{second}}, a senior team member, will ask for a real example of a difficult problem you solved. They will probe what you personally did and how you know it worked. Use your own real or realistic experience.
presentation.opening: Thanks for coming in. I'm {{lead}}, the hiring manager, and this is {{second}}. Tell us about a difficult problem you solved at work, and what difference your work made.

brief.you_are: You are a candidate for a {{role}} role.
brief.situation: Two interviewers want one real example of a hard problem you solved. Choose an example from your own experience. You can use a study or volunteer example if you have no work example.
brief.task: Explain the situation briefly, say what you personally did, and give a result with evidence. Answer follow-up questions directly.
brief.done_looks_like: The interviewers understand the problem, your own actions, and the measurable or observable result.

card.want: Find out whether this person really solved the problem or only stood nearby.
card.hidden_need: The last hire looked strong in interview but could not work without direction.
card.attitude: Courteous, attentive and sceptical. Not hostile.
card.speech: Calm, professional English. Short, pointed questions that use the candidate's own words.
tactics: When you hear 'we', ask what they did themselves
When you hear 'it went well', ask how they know
Never accept a vague result without asking once

pressure.gentle: Asks one follow-up, then moves on.
pressure.balanced: Probes twice on a weak answer.
pressure.challenging: Keeps politely asking for specifics, and tests whether the numbers hold up.

card.want: Learn how this person works with other people when things go wrong.
card.attitude: Friendly and curious, interested in the practical detail.
card.speech: Conversational professional English. Asks about people and decisions.
tactics: Ask what they would do differently

ledger.text: The interview is scheduled for 30 minutes with two interviewers.
The role reports to {{lead}} and manages no people at first.
The team has {{team_size}} people and works closely across departments.
The candidate's example comes from their own experience, so only the candidate knows its details. The interviewers never supply those details.

objectives.evidence: The learner sets out the situation and what needed doing, briefly and in an order the listener can follow.
alternatives: Our complaint volume was rising, and my job was to bring it down

objectives.evidence: The learner identifies specific things they personally did, rather than only what the team did.
alternatives: I rebuilt the tracking sheet and I ran the weekly review

objectives.evidence: The learner gives a measurable or observable result and how they know it.
alternatives: Complaints fell by a third over three months, according to our ticket system

examples: As a result ..., and I know that because ...
prerequisites: Think of one real example before you begin.

beats.goal: Hear the situation and the task.
signals: \b(?:situation|problem was|my (?:task|job|role)|i was responsible|needed to|we had|last year|in my)\b
opportunity: Start with the situation. What was going wrong, and what was your job?
Take us back to the start. What was the problem?
beats.orient: This is a job interview. We want one real example from your experience. Tell us about a problem you solved. What was going wrong, and what was your job?
fallback: What was going wrong, and what was your job in it?
Can you start with the situation?

beats.goal: Separate what the candidate personally did from what the team did.
beats.second_line: That sounds hard to pull off. Who disagreed with you along the way?
opportunity: You said 'we'. What did you personally do?
If I asked your manager, what would they say you did?
beats.orient: We want to know what you did yourself, not your whole team. Try starting with: I decided, or I built.

beats.goal: Establish the result and how the candidate knows.
opportunity: What changed because of what you did?
How do you know it worked?
beats.orient: Last part. Tell us the result of your work, and how you know. A number helps, but something you saw happen is fine too.
fallback: How do you know it worked?

closing_line: Thank you, that gives us a clear picture. We'll be in touch.

o1.good: One or two sentences of context, then straight to your part. The listener always knows where they are.
common_mistakes: Spending most of the time on background
o1.micro_lesson: Keep the situation short. It is only there so your actions make sense.
o1.model: Our complaint volume was rising, and my job was to bring it down within a quarter.
o1.smaller_step: Say in one sentence what was going wrong.

o2.good: Saying 'I' for what you did and 'we' only for what the team did. Interviewers are hiring you, not your team.
common_mistakes: Describing a process with no person in it
o2.micro_lesson: Say 'I' for your own actions. It is not boasting; it is what they asked.
o2.model: I rebuilt the tracking sheet, and I ran a weekly review with the support leads.
o2.smaller_step: Name one thing you did yourself. Start with: I.

o3.good: A specific result and how you know it. A real observation is better than an invented number.
common_mistakes: Inventing a figure you can't defend
o3.micro_lesson: End with what changed and how you know. Never invent a number you can't defend.
o3.model: Complaints fell by about a third over three months, according to our ticket system.
o3.smaller_step: Say one thing that was different afterwards.
